vignette:
He is 49, a North American man who has spent most of his adult life designing buildings meant to feel safe, ordered, and predictable. He is an architect, the kind who notices sightlines, exits, load-bearing walls, and the way people move through space without thinking about it. Before the trauma, he takes pride in this way of seeing. It makes him good at his job. It also makes what happens impossible to forget.

Three years ago, he is leaving a construction site visit in the late afternoon, still wearing his hard hat and carrying rolled drawings under one arm. A steel delivery truck is backing into the narrow service lane beside the project. Across the lane, a younger worker he has seen on and off through the build is crossing between stacked materials, talking to someone over his shoulder. He remembers noticing, almost automatically, that the driver’s line of sight is blocked. He opens his mouth to shout, but the moment moves faster than he does. There is the mechanical beep of the truck, a burst of yelling, then the sickening impact. He watches the worker go down under the rear wheels. For a second everything is silent to him except the beeping, which continues with a grotesque regularity. He sees the worker’s hard hat roll away in a half-circle and stop against a curb.

He runs forward and then stops, frozen by what he sees. Other men are shouting for the driver to pull forward, for someone to call 911, for blankets, for space. He kneels because everyone else is kneeling, but his hands hover uselessly. Later he tells himself he should have done more, should have yelled sooner, should have anticipated the blind spot before it became fatal. At the time he cannot think in full sentences. He can only register fragments: the smell of diesel, the dust on the worker’s vest, the driver climbing down from the cab with a face gone white. That night he stands in his shower long after the water turns cold, trying to wash off a feeling he cannot name.

In the weeks afterward, he tells himself he is shaken but functioning. He goes back to work quickly. His colleagues praise him for keeping the project moving after “such a terrible incident.” He nods and discusses revised site logistics, but inside he is waiting for the beeping sound to start again. It does, often when he is falling asleep. He hears backing alarms in dreams and wakes with his heart pounding, already halfway out of bed. Sometimes the image of the rolling hard hat flashes into his mind while he is reviewing drawings with a client. He loses his place mid-sentence and has to pretend he is tired.

Soon he begins arranging his days around avoidance. He delegates site visits whenever he can, especially if heavy vehicles are expected. If he has to go, he arrives early to study access routes and leaves before deliveries start. He no longer parks near loading zones. At home, he takes long alternate routes to avoid roads with roadwork, cranes, or construction staging. His wife first experiences this as irritability. He snaps when she mentions a home renovation, and when a garbage truck backs up outside their house one morning, he slams the window shut so hard it startles them both. He cannot explain why he is suddenly angry all the time. Anger feels easier than admitting fear.

His world grows narrower in ways he hates. He used to take pleasure in walking through half-finished buildings, imagining what they would become. Now unfinished spaces make his skin prickle. He scans constantly for hazards other people do not seem to notice—an unsecured ladder, a reversing forklift, a distracted laborer. During meetings he chooses chairs with a clear view of the door. In restaurants he tracks the waitstaff’s paths and flinches if someone approaches from behind. He sleeps lightly, then not much at all. His wife tells him he thrashes and sometimes shouts “Stop” in his sleep. He starts staying up late over minor drawing revisions because exhaustion feels more manageable than lying in the dark waiting for images he does not want.

He also carries a private, stubborn guilt. Logically, he knows he did not cause the death. He was not the driver, not the site superintendent, not the worker’s foreman. Still, he returns to that single second and edits it endlessly: if he had spoken sooner, if he had walked faster, if he had insisted on a different traffic plan months before. Because he is an architect, he is used to believing that careful planning prevents catastrophe. The randomness of what he witnessed offends his deepest assumptions. He finds himself distrustful of his own competence, reviewing simple decisions over and over. At work, this looks like perfectionism. At home, it looks like standing in the kitchen long after dinner, staring out the window while his wife asks if he heard her.

By the present, he is tired in a way that feels moral as much as physical. He still works, still meets deadlines, still presents polished concepts to clients. Most people see him as controlled and highly capable. His wife sees the cost: the silences, the detours, the way his shoulders tense at the sound of trucks, the way he drifts away from conversations as if pulled backward into another scene. He says he feels as though part of him remains in that service lane, trapped in the second before impact, still trying to shout in time.
